hypotheses.justification: The bound stays true for any f, by reducing to f⁺ = fun x ↦ max (f x) 0. First, the right-hand side is positive: hqM gives 2A ≤ M·m, so M·m/(2A) ≥ 1, the log is ≥ 0, and RHS ≥ 2A > 0. Next, f⁺ satisfies every other hypothesis. It is measurable. For a > 0, {f⁺ > a} = {f > a}, so HasWeakL1Bound μ A f⁺ holds (the 0 ≤ A part is unchanged). On s, f⁺ ≤ max M 0 = M, since M ≥ 2A/m > 0. And 0 ≤ f⁺ everywhere. So the existing theorem gives ∫_s f⁺ ≤ RHS. Finally, ∫_s f ≤ ∫_s f⁺. If f is integrable on s, use setIntegral_mono, since f⁺ is integrable on s: it is measurable, lies in [0, M] on s, and μ s < ∞. If f is not integrable on s, then ∫_s f = 0 ≤ ∫_s f⁺. Degenerate cases (μ s = 0, f ≤ 0 on s) are covered by the same argument.

Deleting this alone (keeping hf0) leaves the statement true. Case 1: f is not AEStronglyMeasurable for μ.restrict s. Then ∫_s f = 0 by the junk convention, and 0 < 2A ≤ RHS, because hqM gives M·m/(2A) ≥ 1 and so the log is ≥ 0. Case 2: f is AEStronglyMeasurable. Let h be its measurable version (AEStronglyMeasurable.mk) and set g x = if x ∈ s then max (min (h x) M) 0 else 0. g is measurable because s is measurable (hs). Also g ≥ 0 and g ≤ M on s. Since 0 ≤ f ≤ M on s and h = f a.e. on s, g = f μ.restrict s-a.e., so ∫_s g = ∫_s f. Weak bound for g: for a > 0, {g > a} ⊆ {f > a} ∪ N, where N ⊆ s is the μ-null set where h ≠ f (its μ-measure is at most μ.restrict s {h ≠ f} = 0). So μ{g > a} ≤ μ{f > a}, and HasWeakL1Bound μ A g holds. Applying the theorem to g gives the bound. This hypothesis and hf0 can each be removed on its own; the argument for hf uses hf0, so removing both would need the two reductions combined (f⁺ and then the measurable version), which also works.
